name: March 2024 X-class Flare Series

phenomena.details: X1.1 flare on March 23, 2024 at 01:33 UT from AR 13615 drove the March 24 storm; the region produced further X-class flares, including an X1.1 on March 28.
Multiple CMEs from AR 13615 over several days; moderate speeds ~600–900 km/s; compound arrival at Earth.
Severe (G4) storm from CME arrival on March 24-25; Kp 8, Dst approximately −130 nT.
R3 strong radio blackout during X1.1 peak.

impacts.description: R3 radio blackout caused degraded HF communications for several hours; shortwave propagation disturbed across the Americas and Europe.
Aurora visible across the northern United States and Canada during the severe (G4) storm on March 24-25.
Minor GPS positioning degradation (~5–10 m errors) during peak ionospheric disturbance following the X1.1 flare.

papers.title: Severe (G4) Geomagnetic Storms Observed - 24 March 2024
papers.keyFinding: Operational report that the CME launched on 23 March reached Earth at about 14:11 UTC on 24 March and drove severe (G4) geomagnetic storming expected to persist into 25 March.

summary: Late-March 2024 activity from AR 13615 produced X-class flares and a severe (G4) geomagnetic storm on March 24 (Kp 8, Dst ~ −130 nT) – the strongest storm of Solar Cycle 25 up to that point and a precursor to the extreme May 2024 Gannon Superstorm six weeks later.
description: In late March 2024, active region AR 13615 produced a series of M- and X-class flares as Solar Cycle 25 continued its unexpectedly vigorous rise, tracking well above the original 2019 prediction consensus. An X1.1 flare on March 23 (01:33 UT) launched a coronal mass ejection that, together with additional CMEs, drove a severe (G4) geomagnetic storm on March 24–25 – the NOAA SWPC observed G4 conditions with Kp reaching 8 and Dst approximately −130 nT, the strongest storm of the cycle to that date. HF radio communications experienced R3-class disruption during the flares, and aurora was visible across the northern United States and Canada. The same region produced further X-class flaring (including an X1.1 on March 28, after the storm window catalogued here) before rotating off the disk. The episode is now remembered mainly as a harbinger of the extreme May 2024 Gannon Superstorm, which followed six weeks later from an even more productive active region.
